one_liner: Rust generator emitting a C++ two-stage learned index for static sorted arrays; beats STX B+Tree latency and size.
what_it_does: You give it a sorted binary file of uint32, uint64 or f64 keys plus a model spec (e.g. `cubic,linear 262144`) or `--optimize`. It trains a Recursive Model Index offline and writes `<ns>.cpp`, `<ns>.h`, `<ns>_data.h` and parameter files in `rmi_data/`. The generated API is `bool load(dataPath)`, `uint64_t lookup(uint64_t key, size_t* err)` and `cleanup()`. `lookup` returns only an estimated position and a maximum error. It is not a container: you keep the sorted array and do the final bounded search yourself.
how_it_is_fast: It uses a two-stage Recursive Model Index (Kraska et al. 2018). A root model (linear, cubic spline, radix, normal-CDF, etc.) picks one of B leaf models, and that leaf's linear model predicts the key's position in the array. Each leaf's stored maximum error bounds a short binary search. Inference is a few `std::fma` evaluations with at most two cache misses, while a B-tree takes roughly one cache miss per level. The generator packs each leaf's error next to its parameters to save a cache miss, and hard-codes small layers as constants. The CDFShop optimizer (`--optimize`) searches model types and branching factors along the size/error Pareto front.
when_to_use: Immutable or bulk-rebuilt sorted arrays of 32/64-bit unsigned integers or doubles, such as read-only segments, lookup tables or analytics columns, where you look up the same data many times.
Point or lower-bound lookups where you want lower latency than a B+Tree at a fraction of the memory: in SOSD, 181 ns at 48 MB vs 482 ns at 166 MB for STX B+Tree on 200M 32-bit amzn keys.
Key sets with a learnable CDF (SOSD amzn, face, wiki), where the SOSD paper found learned indexes Pareto-optimal up to about 100 MB of index size.
Read-heavy multithreaded lookup: in SOSD's 40-thread test with 50 MB models, RMI was the only learned index to out-throughput the radix lookup table (RBS).
Build pipelines that can absorb an offline train, codegen and recompile step, and can ship the rmi_data/ parameter files with the binary.
when_not_to_use: Any inserts, deletes or updates. Each change means retrain, regenerate and recompile. Use ALEX or LIPP instead.
Pure point lookups with memory to spare: in the same Table 2, CuckooMap (114.5 ns, 1.5 GB) and RobinHash (93.7 ns, 6.1 GB) are faster.
Hard-to-learn key distributions such as OSM Hilbert-curve cell IDs. On osm, no learned index beat a plain radix table, and small RMIs were slower than binary search over the whole array.
String or variable-length keys. Only u32, u64 and f64 inputs are supported, and 32-bit keys gain nothing because model math runs in 64-bit doubles.

Frequent rebuilds or when you need a maintained, tested library. Build was the slowest of the learned indexes (80 s vs 38 s for PGM and 20 s for RS on the largest amzn size), and substantive development stopped in Aug 2020.

integration.dependencies: Generator: Rust/cargo plus crates rayon, memmap 0.7, byteorder, clap 2.33, json, indicatif, env_logger, log, bytesize, approx, superslice, tabular. Generated code: C++ standard library only, plus the rmi_data/ parameter files at runtime.
integration.min_toolchain: Generated code needs C++17 (it uses std::filesystem). The repo's tests build with g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -ffast-math -march=native, add -lstdc++fs for older GCC, and CI installs g++-8. The generator is Rust edition 2018; the minimum Rust version is not documented and CI uses rust:latest.
integration.platforms: Tested only on x86-64 Linux (Xeon Gold 6230 in SOSD, Docker CI). Parameter files are written little-endian and read back with raw ifstream reads, so a little-endian host is assumed. Bounded (--bounded) mode emits __attribute__((packed)), which ties it to GCC/Clang.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Inferred from the generated code: lookup() only reads namespace-level globals set by load(), so concurrent lookups after load() look safe, and SOSD ran it at up to 40 threads. load() and cleanup() must not race with lookups.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false. It is not an ordered map: no inserts, no stored keys or values, and no iteration. It only returns a position estimate plus an error bound into a sorted array you own, and you write the last-mile search.

gotchas: Only two-layer RMIs are implemented. A three-layer spec such as `linear,linear,linear` hits a bare panic!() (issue #5, not in the README). A radix root with branching factor 1-3 panics (issue #3, open), and very small inputs (~100 keys) can trip an assertion in train_two_layer (issue #8, open).

Correctness of the error bound on duplicate keys is in question. Open PR #14 (Jun 2026) says longest_run never records the final run of duplicates, so the per-leaf error bound can come out too small. Open PR #15 says the cargo unit tests no longer compile and that FixDupsIter feeds every model one phantom duplicate row. Neither is merged.

Each generated index is a C++ namespace with global state and is tied to one dataset. Changing the data means regenerating code and recompiling. load() returns false if rmi_data/ is missing, and lookup() before load() reads unset parameters.
Tuning decides performance. The README calls it critical, and poorly sized RMIs can lose to plain binary search. Inference is std::fma-based, and the repo builds with -march=native -ffast-math.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick RMI over RadixSpline (266.58 ns at 4 MB) or PGM-index (326.48 ns at 14 MB) when the lowest static lookup latency matters more than memory, build time and tuning effort; those two are tuned with two knobs and build faster. If you need inserts, use ALEX or LIPP. CARMI reports beating RMI on the SOSD platform, so benchmark it too.
verified_claims_summary: The claim comes from the SOSD paper (PVLDB 14(1), Table 2): 200M 32-bit amzn keys, 10M random lookups, Xeon Gold 6230. There, the fastest CDFShop-tuned RMI took 180.90 ns per lookup at 48 MB, against 482.11 ns at 166 MB for the STX B+Tree, about 2.7x lower latency at about 3.5x less space. The SOSD harness is a CMake Release build with -ffast-math -march=native, but the paper names no compiler, and both hash tables beat RMI on point lookups.
status_note: Listed as active, but the commit log shows no code changes from Aug 2020 until May 2026, when a 2020 cleanup PR (#7, header guards) was merged. Fix PRs #14 and #15 are open. It is MIT-licensed, and the generated C++ is small and dependency-free to vendor, but regenerating needs the Rust toolchain.
